Americas
The Americas, sometimes collectively called America, are a landmass comprising the totality of <color=#3366CC>North America</color> and
<color=#3366CC>South America</color>. When viewed as a single continent, the Americas are the second largest continent by area after Asia
and the third largest continent by population. The Americas make up most of the land in Earth's <color=#3366CC>Western Hemisphere</color>
and constitute the "<color=#3366CC>New World</color>", in contrast to the "<color=#3366CC>Old World</color>" of <color=#3366CC>Afro-Eurasia</color>.
Along with their associated islands, the Americas cover 8% of Earth's total surface area and 28.4% of its land area. The
topography is dominated by the <color=#3366CC>American Cordillera</color>, a long chain of mountains that runs the length of the west coast.
The flatter eastern side of the Americas is dominated by large river basins, such as the Amazon, <color=#3366CC>St. Lawrence</color>
<color=#3366CC>River</color>–<color=#3366CC>Great Lakes</color>, Mississippi, and La Plata basins. Since the Americas extend 14000 km from north to south, the

climate and ecology vary widely, from the arctic <color=#3366CC>tundra</color> of Northern Canada, <color=#3366CC>Greenland</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Alaska</color>, to the <color=#3366CC>tropical</color>
<color=#3366CC>rainforests</color> in <color=#3366CC>Central America</color> and South America.
Humans first <color=#3366CC>settled the Americas</color> from Asia between 20,000 and 16,000 years ago. A second migration of <color=#3366CC>Na-Dene</color>
<color=#3366CC>speakers</color> followed later from Asia. The subsequent migration of the <color=#3366CC>Inuit</color> into the neoarctic c. 3500 BCE completed
what is generally regarded as the settlement by the <color=#3366CC>Indigenous peoples of the Americas</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Norse colonization of</color>
<color=#3366CC>North America</color> saw several settlements established in Greenland, and perhaps on the mainland, however, these were
later abandoned. The Spanish <color=#3366CC>voyages of Christopher Columbus</color> from 1492 to 1504 resulted in permanent contact with
European (and subsequently, other <color=#3366CC>Old World</color>) powers, which eventually led to the <color=#3366CC>Columbian exchange</color> and
inaugurated a period of exploration, <color=#3366CC>conquest, and colonization</color> whose effects and consequences persist to the present.
The Spanish presence involved the enslavement of large numbers of the indigenous population of the Americas.
Diseases introduced from Europe and <color=#3366CC>West Africa</color> devastated the indigenous peoples, and the European powers
<color=#3366CC>colonized the Americas</color>. Mass emigration from Europe, including large numbers of <color=#3366CC>indentured servants</color>, and <color=#3366CC>importation</color>
<color=#3366CC>of African slaves</color> largely replaced the indigenous peoples in much of the Americas. <color=#3366CC>Decolonization of the Americas</color>
began with the <color=#3366CC>American Revolution</color> in the 1770s and largely ended with the <color=#3366CC>Spanish–American War</color> in the late 1890s.
Currently, almost all of the population of the Americas resides in independent countries; however, the legacy of the
colonization and settlement by Europeans is that the Americas share many common cultural traits, most notably
<color=#3366CC>Christianity</color> and the use of West European languages: primarily <color=#3366CC>Spanish</color>, <color=#3366CC>English</color>, Portuguese, French, and, to a lesser
extent, Dutch.
The Americas are home to more than a billion inhabitants, two-thirds of whom reside in the United States, Brazil, and
Mexico. It is home to eight <color=#3366CC>megacities</color> (<color=#3366CC>metropolitan areas</color> with 10 million inhabitants or more): Greater Mexico City
(21.2 million), São Paulo (21.2 million), New York City (19.7 million), Los Angeles (18.8 million), Buenos Aires (15.6
million), Rio de Janeiro (13.0 million), Bogotá (10.4 million), and Lima (10.1 million).
Etymology and naming
The name "America" was first recorded in 1507. A world map created by <color=#3366CC>Martin Waldseemüller</color> was the earliest
recorded use of the term. The name was also used (together with the related term Amerigen) in the Cosmographiae
Introductio, apparently written by <color=#3366CC>Matthias Ringmann</color>, in reference to South America. It was applied to both North and
South America by <color=#3366CC>Gerardus Mercator</color> in 1538. "America" derives from Americus, the Latin version of the Italian explorer
<color=#3366CC>Amerigo Vespucci</color>'s first name.
The feminine form America was originally used to refer to the newly discovered continent, which is why it was accorded
with the feminine names of the other continents: <color=#3366CC>Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Africa</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Europa</color>.
Since the 1950s, however, North America and South America have generally been considered by English speakers as
separate continents, and taken together are called the Americas, or more rarely America. When conceived as a unitary
continent, the form is generally the continent of America in the singular. However, without a clarifying context, singular
America in English commonly refers to the <color=#3366CC>United States of America</color>.
Terminology
History
The region was initially termed America or New India on the Mercator maps.
English
Speakers of <color=#3366CC>English</color> generally refer to the landmasses of North America and South America as the Americas, the
<color=#3366CC>Western Hemisphere</color>, or the <color=#3366CC>New World</color>. The adjective American may be used to indicate something pertaining to the
Americas, but this term is primarily used in English to indicate something pertaining to the United States. Some
non-ambiguous alternatives exist, such as the adjective Pan-American, or New Worlder as a demonym for a resident of
the closely related New World. Use of America in the hemispherical sense is sometimes retained, or can occur when
translated from other languages. For example, the Association of National Olympic Committees (ANOC) in Paris
maintains a single continental association for "America", represented by one of the five Olympic rings.
American essayist <color=#3366CC>H. L. Mencken</color> said, "The Latin-Americans use Norteamericano in formal writing, but, save in
Panama, prefer nicknames in colloquial speech." To avoid "American" one can use constructed terms in their
languages derived from "United States" or even "North America". In Canada, its southern neighbor is often referred to
as "the United States", "the U.S.A.", or (informally) "the States", while U.S. citizens are generally referred to as
"Americans". Most Canadians resent being referred to as "Americans".
Spanish
In Spanish, América is a single continent composed of the <color=#3366CC>subcontinents</color> of América del Sur and América del Norte, the
land bridge of América Central, and the islands of the Antillas. Americano or americana in Spanish refers to a person
from América in a similar way that in which europeo or europea refers to a person from Europa. The terms
sudamericano/a, centroamericano/a, antillano/a and norteamericano/a can be used to more specifically refer to the
location where a person may live.
Citizens of the United States of America are normally referred to by the terms estadounidense and
estadunidense(rough literal translation: "United Statesian") instead of americano or americana which is discouraged,
and the country's name itself is officially translated as Estados Unidos de América (United States of America),
commonly abbreviated as Estados Unidos (EE. UU.). Also, the term norteamericano (North American) may refer to a
citizen of the United States, though in formal writing it is less common since it is used for the inhabitants of North
America.
Portuguese
In Portuguese, is a single continent composed of América do Sul (South America), América Central (Central America)
and América do Norte (North America). It can be ambiguous, as América can be used to refer to the United States of
America, but is avoided in print and formal environments. The demonym 'American' (americano) is commonly used in
Portuguese to refer to people from the United States, although the terms, or also formally exist and are preferred by
those who wish to distinguish it from the continental demonym.
French
In French, the word américain may be used for things relating to the Americas; however, similar to English, it is most
often used for things relating to the United States, with the term états-unien sometimes used for clarity. Panaméricain
may be used as an adjective to refer to the Americas without ambiguity. French speakers may use the noun Amérique
to refer to the whole landmass as one continent, or two continents, Amérique du Nord and Amérique du Sud. In French,
Amérique is seldom used to refer to the United States, leading to some ambiguity when it is. Similar to English usage,
les Amériques or des Amériques is used to refer unambiguously to the Americas.
Dutch
In Dutch, the word Amerika mostly refers to the United States. Although the United States is equally often referred to as
de Verenigde Staten ("the United States") or de VS ("the US"), Amerika relatively rarely refers to the Americas, but it is
the only commonly used Dutch word for the Americas. This often leads to ambiguity; and to stress that something
concerns the Americas as a whole, Dutch uses a combination, namely Noord- en Zuid-Amerika (North and South
America).
Latin America and Central America are generally referred to as Latijns Amerika and Midden-Amerika respectively.
The adjective Amerikaans is most often used for things or people relating to the United States. There are no alternative
words to distinguish between things relating to the United States or to the Americas. Dutch uses the local alternative for
things relating to elsewhere in the Americas, such as Argentijns for Argentine, etc.
History
Pre-Columbian era
The pre-Columbian era incorporates all period subdivisions in the <color=#3366CC>history and prehistory of the Americas</color> before the
appearance of significant European influences on the American continents, spanning the time of the <color=#3366CC>original settlement</color>
in the <color=#3366CC>Upper Paleolithic</color> to <color=#3366CC>European colonization</color> during the <color=#3366CC>Early Modern period</color>. The term Pre-Columbian is used
especially often in the context of the great indigenous civilizations of the Americas, such as those of <color=#3366CC>Mesoamerica</color>

(<color=#3366CC>Olmec</color>, <color=#3366CC>Toltec</color>, <color=#3366CC>Teotihuacano</color>, <color=#3366CC>Zapotec</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mixtec</color>, <color=#3366CC>Aztec</color>, <color=#3366CC>Maya</color>) and the <color=#3366CC>Andean civilizations</color> (<color=#3366CC>Inca</color>, <color=#3366CC>Moche</color>, <color=#3366CC>Chavín</color>,
Muisca, Cañari).
Many pre-Columbian <color=#3366CC>civilizations</color> established characteristics and hallmarks which included permanent or urban
settlements, agriculture, civic and monumental architecture, and complex societal hierarchies. Some of these
civilizations had long faded by the time of the first permanent European arrivals (c. late 15th–early 16th centuries), and
are known only through <color=#3366CC>archeological</color> investigations. Others were contemporary with this period, and are also known
from historical accounts of the time. A few, such as the Maya, had their own written records. However, most Europeans
of the time viewed such texts as pagan, and much was destroyed in Christian pyres. Only a few hidden documents
remain today, leaving modern historians with glimpses of ancient culture and knowledge.
Settlement
<color=#3366CC>The first inhabitants</color> migrated into the Americas from Asia. Habitation sites are known in <color=#3366CC>Alaska</color> and <color=#3366CC>Yukon</color> from at
least 20,000 years ago, with suggested ages of up to 40,000 years. Beyond that, the specifics of the <color=#3366CC>Paleo-Indian</color>
migration to and throughout the Americas, including the dates and routes traveled, are subject to ongoing research and
discussion. Widespread habitation of the Americas occurred after the <color=#3366CC>Late Glacial Maximum</color>, from 16,000 to 13,000
years ago.
The traditional theory has been that these early migrants moved into the <color=#3366CC>Beringia</color> land bridge between eastern Siberia
and present-day Alaska about 40,000–17,000 years ago, when sea levels were significantly lowered during the
<color=#3366CC>Quaternary glaciation</color>. These people are believed to have followed herds of now-extinct <color=#3366CC>pleistocene megafauna</color> along
ice-free corridors that stretched between the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets. Another route proposed is that,
either on foot or using <color=#3366CC>primitive boats</color>, they migrated down the Pacific coast to South America. Evidence of the latter
would since have been covered by a <color=#3366CC>sea level rise</color> of hundreds of meters following the last ice age. Both routes may
have been taken, although the genetic evidences suggests a single founding population. The micro-satellite diversity
and distributions specific to <color=#3366CC>South American Indigenous peoples</color> indicates that certain populations have been isolated
since the initial colonization of the region.
A second migration occurred after the initial peopling of the Americas; <color=#3366CC>Na Dene speakers</color>, found predominantly in North
American groups at varying genetic rates, with the highest frequency found among the Athabaskans at 42%, derive
from this second wave. <color=#3366CC>Linguists</color> and biologists have reached a similar conclusion based on analysis of Amerindian
language groups and <color=#3366CC>ABO blood group system</color> distributions. Then the people of the Arctic small tool tradition, a broad
cultural entity that developed along the <color=#3366CC>Alaska Peninsula</color>, around <color=#3366CC>Bristol Bay</color>, and on the eastern shores of the Bering
Strait c. 2500 BCE, moved into North America. The Arctic small tool tradition, a Paleo-Eskimo culture, branched off into
two cultural variants, including the Pre-Dorset and the Independence traditions of Greenland. The descendants of the
Pre-Dorset cultural group, the Dorset culture, were displaced by the final migrants from the Bering sea coast line, the
Thule people (the ancestors of modern <color=#3366CC>Inuit</color>), by 1000 <color=#3366CC>CE</color>.
Norse colonization
Around the same time as the Inuit migrated into Greenland, Viking settlers began arriving in <color=#3366CC>Greenland</color> in 982 and
Vinland shortly thereafter, establishing a settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows, near the northernmost tip of
<color=#3366CC>Newfoundland</color>. Contact between the Norse colonies and Europe was maintained, as James Watson Curran states:
From 985 to 1410, Greenland was in touch with the world. Then silence. In 1492 the <color=#3366CC>Vatican</color> noted that no news of that
country "at the end of the world" had been received for 80 years, and the bishopric of the colony was offered to a
certain ecclesiastic if he would go and "restore Christianity" there. He didn't go.
Large-scale European colonization
Although there had been previous trans-oceanic contact, large-scale European colonization of the Americas began with
the first voyage of <color=#3366CC>Christopher Columbus</color> in 1492. The first Spanish settlement in the Americas was La Isabela in
northern <color=#3366CC>Hispaniola</color>. This town was abandoned shortly after in favor of <color=#3366CC>Santo Domingo de Guzmán</color>, founded in 1496,
the oldest American city of European foundation. This was the base from which the Spanish monarchy administered its
new colonies and their expansion. Santo Domingo was subject to frequent raids by English and French pirates.
On the continent, <color=#3366CC>Panama City</color> on the Pacific coast of Central America, founded on August 15, 1519, played an
important role, being the base for the Spanish conquest of South America. Conquistador <color=#3366CC>Lucas Vázquez de Ayllón</color>
established San Miguel de Guadalupe, the first European settlement in what is now the <color=#3366CC>United States</color>, on the Pee Dee
River in <color=#3366CC>South Carolina</color>. During the first half of the 16th century, Spanish colonists conducted raids throughout the
Caribbean Basin, bringing captives from Central America, northern South America, and <color=#3366CC>Florida</color> back to Hispaniola and
other Spanish settlements.
France, led by <color=#3366CC>Jacques Cartier</color> and <color=#3366CC>Giovanni da Verrazzano</color>, focused primarily on North America. English explorations
of the Americas were led by <color=#3366CC>Giovanni Caboto</color> and Sir <color=#3366CC>Walter Raleigh</color>. The Dutch in New Netherland confined their
operations to Manhattan Island, Long Island, the Hudson River Valley, and what later became New Jersey. The spread
of new diseases brought by Europeans and African slaves killed many of the inhabitants of North America and South
America, with a general population crash of Native Americans occurring in the mid-16th century, often well ahead of
European contact. One of the most devastating diseases was <color=#3366CC>smallpox</color>.
European immigrants were often part of state-sponsored attempts to found colonies in the Americas. Migration
continued as people moved to the Americas fleeing <color=#3366CC>religious persecution</color> or seeking economic opportunities. Millions of
individuals were forcibly transported to the Americas as <color=#3366CC>slaves</color>, prisoners or <color=#3366CC>indentured servants</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Decolonization of the Americas</color> began with the <color=#3366CC>American Revolution</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Haitian Revolution</color> in the late 1700s. This
was followed by numerous <color=#3366CC>Latin American wars of independence</color> in the early 1800s. Between 1811 and 1825,

<color=#3366CC>Paraguay</color>, <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color>, <color=#3366CC>Chile</color>, <color=#3366CC>Gran Colombia</color>, the <color=#3366CC>United Provinces of Central America</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mexico</color>, <color=#3366CC>Brazil</color>, <color=#3366CC>Peru</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Bolivia</color>
gained independence from Spain and Portugal in armed revolutions. After the <color=#3366CC>Dominican Republic won independence</color>
<color=#3366CC>from Haiti</color>, it was re-annexed by Spain in 1861, but reclaimed its independence in 1865 at the conclusion of the
Dominican Restoration War. The last violent episode of decolonization was the <color=#3366CC>Cuban War of Independence</color> which
became the <color=#3366CC>Spanish–American War</color>, which resulted in the independence of <color=#3366CC>Cuba</color> in 1898, and the transfer of
sovereignty over <color=#3366CC>Puerto Rico</color> from Spain to the United States.
Peaceful decolonization began with the United States's purchase of <color=#3366CC>Louisiana from France</color> in 1803, <color=#3366CC>Florida from Spain</color>
in 1819, <color=#3366CC>Alaska from Russia</color> in 1867, and the Danish West Indies from Denmark in 1916. <color=#3366CC>Canada</color> became independent
of the United Kingdom, starting with the Balfour Declaration of 1926 and the <color=#3366CC>Statute of Westminster 1931</color> and ending
with the patriation of the Canadian Constitution in 1982. The Dominion of Newfoundland similarly achieved
independence under the Balfour Declaration and Statute of Westminster, but relinquished self-rule in 1934. It was
subsequently confederated with Canada in 1949.
The remaining European colonies in the Caribbean began to achieve peaceful independence well after <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Jamaica</color> and <color=#3366CC>Trinidad and Tobago</color> became independent in 1962, and <color=#3366CC>Guyana</color> and <color=#3366CC>Barbados</color> both achieved

independence in 1966. In the 1970s, the <color=#3366CC>Bahamas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Grenada</color>, <color=#3366CC>Dominica</color>, <color=#3366CC>St. Lucia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>St. Vincent and the Grenadines</color>
all became independent of the United Kingdom, and <color=#3366CC>Suriname</color> became independent of the Netherlands. <color=#3366CC>Belize</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Antigua and Barbuda</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Saint Kitts and Nevis</color> achieved independence from the United Kingdom in the 1980s.
Geography
Extent
The Americas make up most of the land in Earth's <color=#3366CC>Western Hemisphere</color>. The northernmost point of the Americas is
Kaffeklubben Island, which is the most northerly point of land on Earth. The southernmost undisputed point is Águila
Islet, although the <color=#3366CC>Antarctic</color> islands of Southern Thule are sometimes taken into account. The mainland of the Americas
is the world's longest north-to-south landmass. The distance between its two polar extremities, Murchison Promontory
on the Boothia Peninsula in northern Canada and Cape Froward in Chilean <color=#3366CC>Patagonia</color>, is roughly 14000 km. The
mainland's most westerly point is the end of the <color=#3366CC>Seward Peninsula</color> in Alaska; <color=#3366CC>Attu Island</color>, further off the Alaskan coast
to the west, is considered the westernmost point of the Americas. Ponta do Seixas in northeastern Brazil forms the
easternmost extremity of the mainland, while Nordostrundingen, in Greenland, is the most easterly point of the
continental shelf.
Geology
South America broke off from the west of the supercontinent <color=#3366CC>Gondwana</color> about 135 million years ago, forming its own
continent. About 15 million years ago, the collision of the <color=#3366CC>Caribbean Plate</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Plate</color> resulted in the
emergence of a series of volcanoes along the border that created a number of islands. The gaps in the archipelago of
Central America filled in with material eroded off North America and South America, plus new land created by
continued volcanism. By three million years ago, the continents of North America and South America were linked by the
<color=#3366CC>Isthmus of Panama</color>, thereby forming the single landmass of the Americas. The Great American Interchange resulted in

many species being spread across the Americas, such as the <color=#3366CC>cougar</color>, <color=#3366CC>procyonids</color>, porcupines, <color=#3366CC>opossums</color>, <color=#3366CC>armadillos</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>hummingbirds</color>.
Topography
The geography of the western Americas is dominated by the <color=#3366CC>American Cordillera</color>, with the <color=#3366CC>Andes</color> running along the
west coast of South America and the <color=#3366CC>Rocky Mountains</color> and other North American Cordillera ranges running along the
western side of North America. The 2300 km <color=#3366CC>Appalachian Mountains</color> run along the east coast of North America from
<color=#3366CC>Alabama</color> to <color=#3366CC>Newfoundland</color>. North of the Appalachians, the Arctic Cordillera runs along the eastern coast of Canada.

The largest mountain ranges are the <color=#3366CC>Andes</color> and <color=#3366CC>Rocky Mountains</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Sierra Nevada</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Cascade Range</color> reach
similar altitudes as the Rocky Mountains, but are significantly smaller. In North America, the greatest number of
fourteeners are in the United States, and more specifically in the US state of <color=#3366CC>Colorado</color>. The highest peaks of the
Americas are located in the Andes, with <color=#3366CC>Aconcagua</color> of <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color> being the highest; in North America <color=#3366CC>Denali</color> (Mount
McKinley) in the US state of <color=#3366CC>Alaska</color> is the tallest.
Between its coastal mountain ranges, North America has vast flat areas. The Interior Plains spread over much of the
continent, with low relief. The <color=#3366CC>Canadian Shield</color> covers almost 5 million km2 of North America and is generally quite flat.
Similarly, the north-east of South America is covered by the flat Amazon basin. The <color=#3366CC>Brazilian Highlands</color> on the east
coast are fairly smooth but show some variations in landform, while farther south the <color=#3366CC>Gran Chaco</color> and <color=#3366CC>Pampas</color> are
broad <color=#3366CC>lowlands</color>.
Climate
The climate of the Americas varies significantly from region to region. <color=#3366CC>Tropical rainforest climate</color> occurs in the latitudes

of the <color=#3366CC>Amazon</color>, American cloud forests, southeastern Florida and <color=#3366CC>Darién Gap</color>. In the <color=#3366CC>Rocky Mountains</color> and <color=#3366CC>Andes</color>, dry
and continental climates are observed. Often the higher altitudes of these mountains are snow-capped.
Southeastern North America is well known for its occurrence of <color=#3366CC>tornadoes</color> and <color=#3366CC>hurricanes</color>, of which the vast majority of
tornadoes occur in the United States' Tornado Alley, as well as in the southerly Dixie Alley in the North American
late-winter and early spring seasons. Often parts of the Caribbean are exposed to the violent effects of hurricanes.
These weather systems are formed by the collision of dry, cool air from Canada and wet, warm air from the Atlantic.
Hydrology
With coastal mountains and interior plains, the Americas have several large <color=#3366CC>river basins</color> that drain the continents. The
largest river basin in North America is that of the <color=#3366CC>Mississippi</color>, covering the second-largest watershed on the planet. The
Mississippi–Missouri river system drains most of 31 states of the United States, most of the <color=#3366CC>Great Plains</color>, and large
areas between the Rocky and Appalachian mountains. The Mississippi–Missouri is the fourth-longest river system and
has the tenth-greatest discharge in the world.
In North America, to the east of the <color=#3366CC>Appalachian Mountains</color>, there are no major rivers but rather a series of rivers and
streams that flow east with their terminus in the Atlantic Ocean, such as the <color=#3366CC>Hudson</color>, <color=#3366CC>Saint John</color>, and Savannah rivers.
A similar instance arises with central Canadian rivers that drain into <color=#3366CC>Hudson Bay</color>; the largest being the <color=#3366CC>Churchill River</color>.

On the west coast of North America, the main rivers are the <color=#3366CC>Colorado</color>, <color=#3366CC>Columbia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Yukon</color>, <color=#3366CC>Fraser</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Sacramento</color>
rivers.
The Colorado River drains much of the Southern Rockies and parts of the <color=#3366CC>Basin and Range Province</color>. The river flows
approximately 1450 mi into the <color=#3366CC>Gulf of California</color>, during which over time it has carved out natural phenomena such as
the <color=#3366CC>Grand Canyon</color> and created phenomena such as the <color=#3366CC>Salton Sea</color>. The Columbia is a large river, 1243 mi long, in
central western North America and is the most powerful river on the West Coast of the Americas. In the far northwest of
North America, the Yukon drains much of the Alaskan peninsula and flows 1980 mi from parts of Yukon and the
Northwest Territory to the Pacific. Draining to the Arctic Ocean of Canada, the <color=#3366CC>Mackenzie River</color> drains waters from the
Arctic Great Lakes of Arctic Canada, as opposed to the St Lawrence River that drains the Great Lakes of southern
Canada into the Atlantic Ocean. The Mackenzie River is the largest in Canada and drains 1805200 km2.
The largest river basin in South America is that of the Amazon, which has the highest volume flow of any river on Earth.
The second largest watershed of South America is that of the <color=#3366CC>Paraná River</color>, which covers about 2582074 km2.
Ecology
North America and South America began to develop a shared population of flora and fauna about 2.5 million years ago,
when <color=#3366CC>continental drift</color> brought the two continents into contact via the <color=#3366CC>Isthmus of Panama</color>. Initially, the exchange of biota
was roughly equal, with North American genera migrating into South America in about the same proportions as South
American genera migrated into North America. This exchange is known as the Great American Interchange. The
exchange became lopsided after roughly a million years, with the total spread of South American genera into North
America far more limited in scope than the spread of North American genera into South America.
Countries and territories
There are 35 sovereign states in the Americas, as well as an <color=#3366CC>autonomous country</color> of <color=#3366CC>Denmark</color>, three overseas
departments of <color=#3366CC>France</color>, three overseas collectivities of France, and one uninhabited territory of France, eight <color=#3366CC>overseas</color>

<color=#3366CC>territories</color> of the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color>, three <color=#3366CC>constituent countries</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Netherlands</color>, three public bodies of the Netherlands,
two <color=#3366CC>unincorporated territories</color> of the <color=#3366CC>United States</color>, and one uninhabited territory of the United States.
Economy
In exports and imports, in 2020, the United States was the world's second largest exporter (US$1.64 trillion) and the
largest importer (US$2.56 trillion). Mexico was the tenth largest exporter and importer. Canada was the twelfth largest
exporter and importer. Brazil was the 24th largest exporter and the 28th largest importer. Chile was the 45th largest
exporter and the 47th largest importer. Argentina was the 46th largest exporter and the 52nd largest importer.
Colombia was the 54th largest exporter and the 51st largest importer; among others.

The <color=#3366CC>agriculture</color> of the continent is very strong and varied. Countries such as <color=#3366CC>United States</color>, <color=#3366CC>Brazil</color>, <color=#3366CC>Canada</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mexico</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color> are among the largest agricultural producers on the planet. In 2019, the continent dominated the world
production of <color=#3366CC>soy</color> (almost 90% of the world total, with Brazil, the United States, Argentina, Paraguay, Canada and
Bolivia among the 10 largest on the planet), <color=#3366CC>sugarcane</color> (about 55% of the world total, with Brazil, Mexico, the United
States, and Guatemala among the 10 largest on the planet), <color=#3366CC>coffee</color> (about 55% of the world total, with Brazil, Colombia,
Honduras, Peru, and Guatemala among the 10 largest on the planet) and <color=#3366CC>maize</color> (about 48% of the world total, with the
United States, Brazil, Argentina, and Mexico among the 10 largest on the planet). The continent also produces almost
40% of world's <color=#3366CC>orange</color> (with Brazil, the United States, and Mexico among the top 10 producers), about 37% of world's
<color=#3366CC>pineapple</color> (with Costa Rica, Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia among the 10 largest producers), about 35% of world's
<color=#3366CC>lemon</color> (with Mexico, Argentina, Brazil, and the United States among the 10 largest producers) and about 30% of world's
<color=#3366CC>cotton</color> (with the United States, Brazil, Mexico and Argentina among the top 10 producers), among several other
products.
In <color=#3366CC>livestock</color>, the Americas are major producers. In 2018, the continent produced about 45% of the world's <color=#3366CC>beef</color> (with the
United States, Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, and Canada among the world's 10 largest producers); about 36% of the
world's <color=#3366CC>chicken meat</color> (with the United States, Brazil, and Mexico among the world's 10 largest producers), and about
28% of the world's <color=#3366CC>cow's milk</color> (with the United States and Brazil among the 10 largest producers in the world), among
other products.
In industrial terms, the <color=#3366CC>World Bank</color> lists the top producing countries each year, based on the total value of production.
According to the 2019 list, the United States has the second most valuable industry in the world (US$2.3 trillion),
Mexico has the 12th most valuable industry in the world (US$217.8 billion), Brazil has the 13th most valuable industry
in the world (US$173.6 billion), Canada has the 15th most valuable industry in the world (US$151.7 billion), Venezuela
the 30th largest (US$58.2 billion, but depends on the oil to obtain this amount), Argentina was the 31st largest
(US$57.7 billion), Colombia the 46th largest (US$35.4 billion), Peru the 50th largest ($28.7 billion), and Chile the 51st
largest (US$28.3 billion), among others.
In the production of <color=#3366CC>oil</color>, the continent had 8 of the 30 largest world producers in 2020: United States (1st), Canada (4th),
Brazil (8th), Mexico (14th), Colombia (20th), Venezuela (26th), Ecuador (27th), and Argentina (28th).
In the production of <color=#3366CC>natural gas</color>, the continent had 8 of the 32 largest world producers in 2015: United States (1st),
Canada (5th), Argentina (18th), Trinidad and Tobago (20th), Mexico (21st), Venezuela (28th), Bolivia (31st), and Brazil
In the production of <color=#3366CC>coal</color>, the continent had 5 of the 30 largest world producers in 2018: United States (3rd), Colombia
(12th), Canada (13th), Mexico (24th), and Brazil (27th).
In the production of <color=#3366CC>vehicles</color>, the continent had 5 of the 30 largest world producers in 2019: United States (2nd), Mexico
(7th), Brazil (9th), Canada (12th), and Argentina (28th).
In the production of <color=#3366CC>steel</color>, the continent had 5 of the 31 largest world producers in 2019: United States (4th), Brazil
(9th), Mexico (15th), Canada (18th), and Argentina (31st).
In <color=#3366CC>mining</color>, the continent has large productions of <color=#3366CC>gold</color> (mainly in the United States, Canada, Peru, Mexico, Brazil, and
Argentina); <color=#3366CC>silver</color> (mainly in Mexico, Peru, Chile, Bolivia, Argentina, and the United States); <color=#3366CC>copper</color> (mainly in Chile,
Peru, the United States, Mexico, and Brazil); <color=#3366CC>platinum</color> (Canada and the United States); <color=#3366CC>iron ore</color> (Brazil, Canada, the
United States, Peru, and Chile); <color=#3366CC>zinc</color> (Peru, the United States, Mexico, Bolivia, Canada, and Brazil); <color=#3366CC>molybdenum</color>
(Chile, Peru, Mexico, Canada, and the United States); <color=#3366CC>lithium</color> (Chile, Argentina, Brazil, and Canada); <color=#3366CC>lead</color> (Peru, the
United States, Mexico, and Bolivia); <color=#3366CC>bauxite</color> (Brazil, Jamaica, Canada, and the United States); <color=#3366CC>tin</color> (Peru, Bolivia, and
Brazil); <color=#3366CC>manganese</color> (Brazil and Mexico); <color=#3366CC>antimony</color> (Bolivia, Mexico, Guatemala, Canada, and Ecuador); <color=#3366CC>nickel</color>
(Canada, Brazil, Dominican Republic, Cuba, and the United States); <color=#3366CC>niobium</color> (Brazil and Canada); <color=#3366CC>rhenium</color> (Chile and
the United States); and <color=#3366CC>iodine</color> (Chile), among others.
<color=#3366CC>Dominica</color>, <color=#3366CC>Panama</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Dominican Republic</color> have the fastest-growing economy in the Americas according to the
<color=#3366CC>International Monetary Fund</color> (IMF), 16, five to seven countries in the southern part of the Americas had weakening
economies in decline, compared to only three countries in the northern part of the Americas. Haiti has the lowest GDP
per capita in the Americas, although its economy was growing slightly as of 2016.
Demographics
Population
In 2021 the total population of the Americas was about 1.03 billion people, divided as follows:
• North America: 596.6 million (includes Central America and the <color=#3366CC>Caribbean</color>)
• South America: 434.3 million
Largest urban centers
There are three urban centers that each hold titles for being the largest population area based on the three main
demographic concepts:
• City proper
A city proper is the locality with legally fixed boundaries and an administratively recognized urban status that is usually
characterized by some form of local government.
• <color=#3366CC>Urban area</color>
An urban area is characterized by higher population density and vast human features in comparison to areas
surrounding it. Urban areas may be cities, towns or conurbations, but the term is not commonly extended to rural
settlements such as villages and hamlets. Urban areas are created and further developed by the process of
urbanization and do not include large swaths of rural land, as do metropolitan areas.
• <color=#3366CC>Metropolitan area</color>
Unlike an urban area, a metropolitan area includes not only the urban area, but also satellite cities plus intervening rural
land that is socio-economically connected to the urban core city, typically by employment ties through commuting, with
the urban core city being the primary labor market.
In accordance with these definitions, the three largest population centers in the Americas are: <color=#3366CC>Mexico City</color>, anchor to
the largest metropolitan area in the Americas; New York City, anchor to the largest urban area in the Americas; and
São Paulo, the largest city proper in the Americas. All three cities maintain Alpha classification and large scale
influence.
Ethnology
The population of the Americas is made up of the descendants of four large <color=#3366CC>ethnic groups</color> and their combinations.
• The <color=#3366CC>Indigenous peoples of the Americas</color>, being Amerindians and <color=#3366CC>Inuit</color>-Yupik-Unangan.

• Those of European ancestry, mainly Spanish, English, Irish, <color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color>, <color=#3366CC>German</color>, <color=#3366CC>Italian</color>, <color=#3366CC>French</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Dutch</color>.
• Those of African ancestry, mainly of West African descent.
• <color=#3366CC>Asians</color>, that is, those of <color=#3366CC>East Asian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asian</color>, and <color=#3366CC>South Asian</color> ancestry.
• <color=#3366CC>Mestizos</color> (Métis people in Canada), those of mixed European and Amerindian ancestry.
• Mulattoes, people of mixed African and European ancestry.
• <color=#3366CC>Zambos</color> (Spanish) or Cafuzos (Portuguese), those of mixed African and Indigenous ancestry.
The majority of the population lives in <color=#3366CC>Latin America</color>, named for its predominant cultures, rooted in Latin Europe
(including the two dominant languages, Spanish and <color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color>, both <color=#3366CC>Romance languages</color>), more specifically in the
<color=#3366CC>Iberian</color> nations of <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color> and Spain (hence the use of the term Ibero-America as a synonym). Latin America is
typically contrasted with <color=#3366CC>Anglo-America</color>, where English, a <color=#3366CC>Germanic language</color>, is prevalent, and which comprises
Canada (with the exception of Francophone Canada rooted in Latin Europe [France]—see <color=#3366CC>Quebec</color> and <color=#3366CC>Acadia</color>) and
the United States. Both countries are located in North America, with cultures deriving predominantly from British and
other <color=#3366CC>Germanic</color> roots.
Black population
The transatlantic slave trade brought millions of Africans to the territories of the Americas under the colonial rule of
European powers, especially South America. In South America, <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color> played a significant role in the trafficking of
enslaved Africans, with estimates suggesting that about 40% of all Africans forcibly brought to the Americas were taken
to Brazil alone, to work primarily in sugar cane plantations, mining, and agricultural endeavors. In North America, the
<color=#3366CC>British Empire</color> was heavily involved in the transatlantic slave trade, with the establishment of colonies such as Virginia,
where enslaved Africans were primarily used as labor in tobacco plantations and later in other agricultural and domestic
sectors. This system perpetuated for centuries, shaping the socio-economic landscape of all nations of the hemisphere.
After the <color=#3366CC>Haitian Revolution</color> led by <color=#3366CC>Jean-Jacques Dessalines</color>, which started in 1791 and was the only successful slave

Religion
The most prevalent faiths in the Americas are as follows:
• Christianity (86 percent)
• Roman Catholicism: Practiced by 69 percent of the Latin American population (61 percent in Brazil whose Roman
Catholic population of 134 million is the greatest of any nation's), approximately 24 percent of the United States'
population and about 39 percent of Canada's.
• Protestantism: Practiced mostly in the United States, where half of the population are Protestant, Canada, with
slightly more than a quarter of the population, and Greenland; there is a growing contingent of <color=#3366CC>Evangelical</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Pentecostal</color> movements in predominantly Catholic Latin America.
• <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodoxy</color>: Found mostly in the United States (1 percent) and Canada; this Christian group is growing
faster than many other Christian groups in Canada and now represents roughly 3 percent of the Canadian
population.
• Non-denominational Christians and other Christians (some 1,000 different Christian denominations and sects
practiced in the Americas).
• <color=#3366CC>Irreligion</color>: About 12 percent, including atheists and agnostics, as well as those who profess some form of spirituality
but do not identify themselves as members of any organized religion.
• Islam: Together, Muslims constitute about 1 percent of the North American population and 0.3 percent of all Latin
Americans. It is practiced by 3 percent of Canadians and 0.6 percent of the U.S. population. <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color> has the
largest Muslim population in Latin America with up to 600,000 persons, or 1.5 percent of the population.
• Judaism: Practiced by 2 percent of North Americans—approximately 2.5 percent of the U.S. population and 1.2
percent of Canadians—as well as 0.23 percent of Latin Americans. Argentina has the largest Jewish population in
Latin America with 200,000 members.

Other faiths include <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>; <color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color>; <color=#3366CC>Sikhism</color>; <color=#3366CC>Baháí Faith</color>; a wide variety of indigenous religions, many of which

can be categorized as <color=#3366CC>animistic</color>; <color=#3366CC>new age</color> religions and many <color=#3366CC>African</color> and African-derived religions. <color=#3366CC>Syncretic</color> faiths can
also be found throughout the Americas.
Languages
Various <color=#3366CC>languages</color> are spoken in the Americas. Some are of European origin, others are spoken by indigenous peoples
or are the mixture of various languages like the different creoles.

The most widely spoken <color=#3366CC>first language</color> in the Americas is <color=#3366CC>Spanish</color>, followed by <color=#3366CC>English</color> and <color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color>. The dominant
language of <color=#3366CC>Latin America</color> is Spanish, though the most populous nation in Latin America, <color=#3366CC>Brazil</color>, speaks Portuguese.
Small enclaves of <color=#3366CC>French</color>-, <color=#3366CC>Dutch</color>- and English-speaking regions also exist in Latin America, notably in <color=#3366CC>French Guiana</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Suriname</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Belize</color> and <color=#3366CC>Guyana</color> respectively. <color=#3366CC>Haitian Creole</color> is dominant in the nation of <color=#3366CC>Haiti</color>, where French is also
spoken. Native languages are more prominent in Latin America than in <color=#3366CC>Anglo-America</color>, with <color=#3366CC>Nahuatl</color>, <color=#3366CC>Quechua</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Aymara</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Guaraní</color> as the most common. Various other native languages are spoken with less frequency across
both Anglo-America and Latin America. <color=#3366CC>Creole languages</color> other than Haitian Creole are also spoken in parts of Latin
America.
The dominant language of Anglo-America is English. French is also official in <color=#3366CC>Canada</color>, where it is the predominant
language in <color=#3366CC>Quebec</color> and an official language in <color=#3366CC>New Brunswick</color> along with English. It is also an important language in
<color=#3366CC>Louisiana</color>, and in parts of <color=#3366CC>New Hampshire</color>, <color=#3366CC>Maine</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Vermont</color>. Spanish has kept an ongoing presence in the

<color=#3366CC>Southwestern United States</color>, which formed part of the <color=#3366CC>Viceroyalty of New Spain</color>, especially in <color=#3366CC>California</color> and <color=#3366CC>New</color>
<color=#3366CC>Mexico</color>, where a distinct variety of Spanish spoken since the 17th century has survived. It has more recently become
widely spoken in other parts of the <color=#3366CC>United States</color> because of heavy immigration from Latin America. High levels of
immigration in general have brought great linguistic diversity to Anglo-America, with over 300 languages known to be
spoken in the United States alone, but most languages are spoken only in small enclaves and by relatively small
immigrant groups.
The nations of Guyana, Suriname, and Belize are generally considered not to fall into either Anglo-America or Latin
America because of their language differences from Latin America, geographic differences from Anglo-America, and
cultural and historical differences from both regions; English is the primary language of Guyana and Belize, and Dutch
is the primary language of Suriname.
Most of the non-native languages have, to different degrees, evolved differently from the mother country, but are
usually still mutually intelligible. Some have combined, however, which has even resulted in completely new languages,
such as Papiamento, which is a combination of Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch (representing the respective colonizers),
native <color=#3366CC>Arawak</color>, various African languages, and, more recently English. The <color=#3366CC>lingua franca</color> Portuñol, a mixture of
Portuguese and Spanish, is spoken in the border regions of Brazil and neighboring Spanish-speaking countries. More
specifically, Riverense Portuñol is spoken by about 100,000 people in the border regions of Brazil and <color=#3366CC>Uruguay</color>.
Because of <color=#3366CC>immigration</color>, there are many communities where other languages are spoken from all parts of the world,
especially in the United States, Brazil, <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color>, Canada, <color=#3366CC>Chile</color>, <color=#3366CC>Costa Rica</color>, and Uruguay—very important
destinations for immigrants.

<color=#3366CC>Baseball</color> is one of the most popular sports in the Americas, having spread through the hemisphere after the growth of

<color=#3366CC>Football</color> is perhaps the most popular and followed sport in the Americas. The North American region which also
includes the Central and Caribbean national associations is overseen by CONCACAF, while the South American region
